title: What does the World Bank's 2026 poverty report actually show about India, and why do economists still disagree?
standfirst: India's estimated extreme poverty rate fell to 2.29% in 2024. Yet 78.78% remained below $8.30 a day. The World Bank's new tables show how both can be true, and where survey changes, welfare valuation and jobs simulations need a more careful reading.
short: The World Bank's 2024 calendar-year estimates put 2.29% of Indians below $3 a day and 78.78% below $8.30, in 2021 PPP prices. Direct survey-year readings differ.
About 76.5% of Indians lie between those lines in the report's binned 2024 distribution. A low extreme-poverty rate does not establish economic security or adequate nutrition.
Survey redesign, PPP revisions and welfare imputation affect measurement. Comparing different poverty lines cannot isolate a questionnaire effect.
The combined jobs counterfactual lowers $8.30 poverty by 22.17 percentage points. It is an accounting exercise, not a forecast or a causal policy estimate.
macha: India has made a large dent in extreme poverty. That still leaves most households below the higher benchmark used for upper-middle-income countries. The distinction matters for a family trying to pay for healthcare or survive a spell without work. Poor paid workers already put in about 44 hours a week. The question is what those hours buy them, and how much of their security a consumption survey can actually see.
caveats: Calendar-year lineup estimates and direct survey years differ. Values after 2024 in the national trajectories are projections or nowcasts, not additional household surveys.
The societal-poverty series uses direct survey years alongside annual lined-up fixed poverty lines. The comparison preserves their different timing and methods.
HCES redesigned interviews and item lists across survey rounds. Models that bridge the break depend on assumptions; their estimates are not interchangeable with direct survey readings.
The Prosperity Gap averages individual ratios of the prosperity standard to consumption. It is not a multiplier for the average household.
The welfare chart uses published sector averages only. The earlier fractile reconstruction required unfrozen microdata and has been removed.
Nutrition, monetary poverty, multidimensional deprivation and medical hardship use different populations and vintages. Their percentages overlap and cannot be added.
The employment comparisons describe groups at each date; households can move between groups. The combined jobs counterfactual does not identify the causal effect of an intervention.

The consumption-loss exercise is a hypothetical uniform reduction in the same 2024 population bins, not a forecast or household transition probability. Its baseline approximates the national lineup at about 0.1 percentage-point resolution.
Decile growth compares repeated cross-sections in PIP’s explicitly comparable HCES rounds. It does not follow the same households or fully measure affluent Indians.

The child comparison uses SPID direct survey estimates, with nested ages 0-5 and all-age populations. It is separate from the GSAP calendar lineup used for the state map; no national child count is inferred.
The selected Asian comparison holds calendar year and PPP lines fixed, but Indonesia is marked actual and the other four countries projection. These are not all in one income group.
